title: Ask HN: Why is AWS such a pain for using Bedrock?
summary:
So we've been granted with AWS Credits which we would like to use for our product, fair and square. Though the terms say you can use them for inference on AWS, this is actually not the case: Anthropic, OpenAI, Kimi, and ZLM are all blocked by an unpublished policy ("not available for this account") Yes, we're not the first who needs exactly those. So our Account Manager submitted a request to allow using them. The account was reviewed for several days and they came back with "Prior requesting an increase on capabilities you must first utilize for some time the current availability on your resources." Kafkaesque. I mean, how can we utilize something we can't use? How did you manage to get access to those models?

title: Pepperwind, a fictional company dataset with 223 tables and 79M rows
summary:
Hi HN. I'm a software engineer, building Misata Studio.

Pepperwind Trading Co, is a fictional spice and tea trader from Kochi, selling in India, Europe and the US for three years. It has a storefront, a subscription club, a warehouse, ledgers in 3 currencies, support, CRM, marketing, product analytics, HR, payroll and company mail. It is around 223 tables, 79 M rows that is around 7GB of parquet files. It was made with the help of the backend engine behind misata studio.

What I found while I was researching about the synthetic dataset needs was that products that is being built for interconnected systems or analytical solutions that serve organisations often lack a real usable test dataset that is realistic enough to verify the performance and workflows accurately. And most of the time synthetic datasets don't care about entity resolution, same customers existing in different places and in different IDs, FKs pointing at rows that doesnt exist, the values might not match exactly and this is a mess when it comes to finances of the datasets. There are plenty out there, but a single heavy and massive dataset is rare. It was from a similar pain that the idea behind building misata was born.

Some things I was focussed on while building Pepperwind was for it to have unique and valuable usability for different usecases, like: - The books balance in the ledger. - 20 incidents planted in. Courier failure in Diwali, Dutch VAT charged on EU invoices, a referral fraud, price rise that pushes subscription churn etc. I made these incidents consistent across the systems. - It ships with 92 KPIs and their values each month, along with 420 questions that can be asked against the dataset.

Misata is a from scratch multi-table synthetic data generation project with an open-source python library and a web tool I am developing for prompt to dataset generation. I had posted about this in December and have come a long way since then https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46289055.

The page lets you explore a small slice of the dataset in your browser and you can follow a single customer through every system. The preview is free and the full version is paid for now, to cover the building cost ($30). Listed in huggingface under CC by 4.0 license: https://huggingface.co/datasets/misatadata/pepperwind .

I would like to reach out to people across dozens of use cases. What would you use it for and how could this or another dataset similar to this help you build your product/solution?

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50333045

Hello,

In the coming weeks, we’ll start testing a combined experience for Chat and Work tabs in ChatGPT with a small group of users. We’ll use their feedback to improve the experience before bringing it to more people.

This will enable you to move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, all in one place. You can bring in your files and plugins and ask ChatGPT to build a website, create a presentation, or do things for you on the web, while reviewing and guiding its work. Codex will remain a separate experience in the ChatGPT desktop app.

As part of this unified experience, your use of ChatGPT and Codex will draw from the same allowance in the coming weeks. Usage will depend on model and task, with more advanced models and complex tasks using more of your allowance. Unlimited Instant is included in your plan and will not draw from your usage.

title: Ask HN: Pivoting from Platform Engineering
summary:
I'm struggling and I hope this message gets some traction.

Are we Platform Engineers / DevOps Engineers done for?

I've been in "Platform Engineering" since it was "Unix Admin", popping Dells and Sun boxes into racks and managing full automation to bring them up to some flavor of server, to 'Systems Engineer' where you write Perl or Java code for a Fortune 50 for some product you integrated to 'DevOps Engineer' where you write terraform and manage EKS to 'Platform Engineering' where you do all those things (minus datacenter), but also are an SRE, a pipeline expert, and a 'software engineer'.

Now, companies are looking for a unicorn and there doesn't appear to be job mobility, you are either getting huge 4-500k offers for Head of roles or nothing at all. Managers are expected to be 100% hands-on, have majored in math or comp-sci, and still have the same preparation as an IC.

I believe that I've aged out of the job market (40's here) because I'm in one of the hottest areas of the U.S. and I get ZERO responses to job applications.

I think that software engineers moving into the space, AI prompting thinking that we can reduce headcount, and a sluggish job market are contributing.

Is anyone pivoting away from these? If so, to what? If not, are you now an 'AI Platform Engineer'? Retired?

(Writing from a burner account, of course.)

title: Can light be used to cyberattack?
summary:
This morning I read an article about Flock cameras in Atlanta, so i started wondering if light could be used to interact with a camera backwards into a digital system?

What I was actually thinking - "How would someone shut down a surveillance camera?"

Optical Cyber Intrusion. Whoa.

Then I started spitballing (thats about my tech level on this topic. OK, fair. Any tech topic.)

Evidently, light can be used to communicate with digital systems. I found a bit of research, like a 2019 paper called aIR-Jumper, which showed communication with air-gapped systems through infrared signals and surveillance cameras.

The next "obvious" question I wondered about was - could light be used as a way to cyberattack? Could an optical signal of some sort be used to disrupt or compromise surveillance cameras or other another connected device? I mean there are so many sites with surveillance sytems, I would imagine theyre all connected into the the company or site network.

Anyone working in optical communications, embedded security, camera systems, or related fields have any insight?

title: Ask HN: What mistakes did AI make in your codebase?
summary:
In the past few weeks I've beeing working with frontier AI - Opus 5.5, Astra, Sol 6.1, Fable 5.1 and Gemini Argon.

AI has become really good at coding in some sense, that's undeniable, and there are people that say you don't really need to review their code anymore.

But I keep getting stuck in a sensation that's between cognitive dissonance, FOMO, and a vague sense of being gaslit, because when I review the code it writes - and this is all of them - 80% of it is right, and 20% is wrong, but in extremely subtle ways; only when you deeply understand the system and carefully review it do you spot the issues. These are not stylistic choices, the code is incorrect. Of course, the AI fixes it when you prompt it to, but you need to work very hard to know what needs prompting.

This is all after the grill-me skills and cross-model adversarial review and whatnot (all these techniques do help somewhat but they didn't get it perfect),

For example, I had AI (Opus 5.5 and Gemini both tried, in this particular case) write an integration test for our system, to reproduce an issue we had. It failed because it chose, for simplicity, to combine two backend fakes into one store, having writes covered by the same mutex, but the bug was only happening in production when these two stores went out of sync (and they did because we wrote to both concurrently and one write failed). (I don't want to argue the merits of the design. This is existing code.)

The wrong code it wrote to try and find the issue was carefully written, well organized, function names were reasonable, etc. etc.

I can't be alone in this, but I can't put my finger on what exactly goes wrong in the process.

Can you share examples of changes you wanted to make that Claude and the bunch (frontier versions) got subtly wrong?

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50328797
